Preprocessing and source alignment

Source: vignettes/articles/preprocessing.Rmd
preprocessing.Rmd

Integration is only as good as the inputs it receives. This page covers the two preprocessing decisions that matter most in MosaiClusteR: how to make heterogeneous sources comparable, and how the sources are aligned so that every method sees the same objects.

The data model

Every source is a numeric matrix with objects (samples) in rows and features in columns. All sources in a List describe the same objects; they may differ in the number of features. This single convention holds for every method, including the M-ABC family, and it is the most common thing to get wrong. If a result looks off, check that a source was not transposed.

library(MosaiClusteR)
data(mosaic_toy)
L <- mosaic_toy$List
vapply(L, dim, integer(2))   # 60 objects in rows; 120 and 150 features

Normalisation

Normalization() rescales a source so that features sit on a comparable scale before a distance is computed. Four strategies are available:

method What it does Use when
"Standardize" centre and scale each feature to unit variance features are on different numeric scales
"Range" rescale each feature to a fixed range you want bounded values and to preserve zeros
"Quantile" map features onto a common quantile distribution distributions differ in shape, not only scale
"Fisher-Yates" rank-based normal-scores transform heavy tails or outliers dominate a raw scale 
Xn <- Normalization(L[[1]], method = "Quantile")

Whether to normalise depends on the source. Expression-style continuous data usually benefits from standardisation or quantile normalisation. Binary data (fingerprints, presence or absence) should not be standardised; pick a distance made for binary data instead (see below).

Distances

Distance() turns a source into an object-by-object dissimilarity. Choose the measure to match the data:

distmeasure For Notes
"euclidean" continuous true Euclidean distance via stats::dist; applies feature normalisation when normalize = is set
"manhattan" continuous sum of absolute differences
"tanimoto", "jaccard" binary overlap of present features
"hamming" binary or categorical count of disagreements
"gower" mixed-type handles continuous and categorical columns together
"cont tanimoto", "MCA_coord" specialised continuous Tanimoto; coordinates from multiple correspondence analysis 
D1 <- Distance(Xn, distmeasure = "euclidean")       # from already-normalised data
round(as.matrix(D1)[1:4, 1:4], 2)

Two equivalent paths give the same result for "euclidean": normalise first and pass the normalised matrix to Distance(), or let Distance() normalise internally with its normalize = argument. Do one or the other, not both.

Preprocess once, or let the method do it

Integration methods accept per-source preprocessing arguments, so you rarely have to preprocess by hand. A method call carries one entry per source for distmeasure, normalize and method:

S  <- length(L)
DM <- rep("euclidean", S)       # one distance per source
NM <- rep(FALSE, S)             # normalise? one flag per source
ME <- rep(list(NULL), S)        # normalisation method per source (NULL = none)

SNF(L, type = "data", distmeasure = DM, normalize = NM, method = ME)

If you have already built dissimilarities yourself, pass them with type = "dist" and the method skips its own distance step.

How sources are aligned

Before combining sources, MosaiClusteR matches them object by object:

  • Row names present: sources are aligned by object name. Rows in a different order are realigned to the first source, so order does not matter.
  • No row names: sources are combined positionally (row 1 with row 1, and so on), so they must already be in the same order.
  • Mismatched sets, different row counts, or duplicated names: these raise a clear error that names the problem, rather than failing later with a cryptic message.

The practical rule: give every source the same object row names. Then you can reorder rows freely and trust the alignment.

Samples missing from a source

If some samples are measured in only part of the sources, use NEMO(). It is the one method here that does not require every object in every source: it averages neighbourhood affinities over the omics that measured each pair, with no imputation. Every other method expects the complete, aligned set.

Mixing data types across sources

Because the methods accept precomputed dissimilarities, you can integrate sources of different kinds. Compute a binary distance on a fingerprint source and a continuous distance on an expression source, then pass both as distance matrices:

Dfp <- Distance(fingerprints, distmeasure = "tanimoto")
Dex <- Distance(Normalization(expression, "Standardize"), distmeasure = "euclidean")
WeightedClust(list(Dfp, Dex), type = "dist", weight = seq(1, 0, -0.25))
